differential.method: the real analyzer against an INDEPENDENT flat-sweep grammar oracle: flat maximal-consecutive-run scan with byte-range suppression, versus the analyzer's recursive descent with threaded lexical scope. Two implementations, deliberately different, so agreement is evidence rather than a restatement.
differential.residual: 2 occurrences, 1 file: terragrunt/test/fixtures/catalog/local-template/.boilerplate/terragrunt.hcl is a Go text/template named .hcl; `{{- range .requiredVariables }}` parses as a binary operation and reads as a two-segment path. Ruled (HCL-D3): the emission is faithful to the bytes, and suppressing it would mean keying on the template words if/range/with, which are also legal HCL identifier bases.

grammarPin.sourceVsWasm: all 64 declared names present (0 supertypes hidden by design), 64 wasm-named types all declared, 0 built-in extras
grammarPin.verdict: PIN AS-IS. The wired bytes ARE a build of the vendored source, so the Groovy situation — a vendored wasm drifted from upstream and repaired by hand — does NOT apply to HCL. 1.2.0 is the only release of the only published HCL grammar package and the repository is not archived, so there is nothing better to move to; the pin's value is provenance and drift detection.
grammarPin.rebuildable: src/parser.c is vendored (600 KB), so `tree-sitter build --wasm` in grammars/tree-sitter-hcl reproduces the wired bytes without a network fetch.
grammarPin.note: the gate currently reports 3 failures, ALL in the nim lane (another agent's live edits to grammars/tree-sitter-nim/grammar.js). HCL: 0. The gate catching that drift is the instrument working.

suppressed for_cond, losing 29 more — the `if ...` tail of a for-expression is an ordinary expression over ordinary references

instrumentDefectsNote: every one of these made the ANALYZER look worse than it is, and one made a correct fix look like a 476-edge regression. They are recorded because the final 0.999931/1.000000 is only as good as the instrument that produced it.

complexity.policy: NO ms-per-file budget is published. Measured under nine concurrent analyzer agents (load average 35-51), the same analyzer over the same 600 files measured 1.451 / 2.097 / 3.885 ms per file on three consecutive rounds — a 2.7x spread on identical work. A single number here measures the neighbours.
complexity.whatIsPublishedInstead: the machine-independent SHAPE of the cost
complexity.ruling: flat ms-per-1k-nodes across size quartiles IS the linearity evidence and the O(n^2) signature is absent. ms-per-byte FALLS with size because fixed per-file overhead amortises — the opposite of a super-linear term. Facts-per-1k-nodes falls 312 -> 219 for the same reason, not because the Set-backed dedupe degrades (a degrading Set would rise).
